1-15231-2-1.subevent: At least four civilians were killed and 10 others were wounded in a mortar attack in northern Faryab province on Thursday morning.
The incident happened around 11:00am local time after a mortar round landed in a market in Shareen Tagab district.
Abdul Karim Yourish, a spokesman for the provincial police chief, said the mortar was fired by the Taliban to target security forces, but all victims were civilians at the market.
The Taliban has not commented on the attack.

0-4495-1-1.subevent: Tunisia Youth Impact uses cooking contests to encourage young Tunisian women in rural villages to vote in the presidential election.
On Saturday, October 12, a cooking contest is held in Echamine, a small rural town south of Tunis, the day before the second round of the presidential election.
The national turnout in the first round was 48.98%, and fewer than half of voters are expected to vote in the second round.
Tunisia Youth Impact's Voticook cooking contests aim to raise awareness among rural populations, especially women, about participating in the democratic process.
The contest simulates real voting conditions, with participants voting for the best dish, and the ink used in real elections replaced by a water and shampoo mixture.
Hinda Jlass, a mother of four, prepares her couscous for the competition and says the event is a way to get together with other women and that participating is essential.
Jlass plans to vote in the presidential election the next day, which would be only the second time she has voted in her life.
Seven women compete in the contest, presenting dishes like couscous, macaroni, and rice, and around fifty people act as electors.
The electors taste the dishes and vote using the same procedure as in the real election, with volunteers guiding them and members of the ISIE and an EU observer present.
After the vote, ballots are counted, and volunteers point out mistakes that could invalidate votes, such as signing instead of crossing next to a candidate.
Najwa Jlass, the hostess's sister, wins the contest and says she is happy to see the community come together and will vote 'for real' the next day.

6-18979-2-t.subevent: Crime adapts to societal changes, evolving from individual opportunistic violations to more differentiated crime structures.
The Sicilian Cosa Nostra adjusted to the shift from a village-agrarian to an urban-industrial economy, changing its investments from land to real property and businesses.
Organized crime has become networks and alliances across national boundaries, linking the underworld with legitimate institutions and white-collar interests.
Drug trafficking leads to corruption, threats, and killings of law enforcement, forces addicts to commit crimes, and launders proceeds into the legal economy.
Organized crime seeks a power monopoly, employing any means for profit without regard for public interest or established rules.
Common criminality and organized crime intersect, but organized crime is distinguished by continuity, hierarchy, and complex operations.
Organized crime develops a mythology of invincibility, which affiliates use to intimidate and threaten.
The reputation of organized crime affects how mafiosi see themselves and are seen by others, with hits signaling inner conflicts.
Defining organized crime is difficult, but informant confessions have provided documentation, as seen with Sicilian Cosa Nostra and Neapolitan camorra.
Nigerian criminal enterprises are pervasive globally, with structures including pyramidal hierarchies, clan networks, and independent cells.
Nigerian criminals target the US and Britain, engaging in heroin trafficking and scams like the '419' advance-fee fraud.
In 1997, Boston authorities arrested a ring of Nigerian check thieves who stole over two billion dollars from banks, law firms, and a brokerage house.
Proceeds from Nigerian crimes finance narcotics smuggling from Thailand and Pakistan to US cities.

0-4931-1-4.subevent: Sheriff Principal Craig Turnbull said the tragedy happened because Captain David Traill had ignored the five fuel warnings he received during the flight.
The police helicopter crashed into the roof of the Clutha bar in Glasgow on 29 November 2013, killing 10 people and injuring 31 others.
The victims' families and the Clutha's owner expressed anger and disappointment at the inquiry's findings, with Mark O'Prey's father saying Capt Traill had been made a 'fall guy'.
During the fatal accident inquiry, Sheriff Turnbull heard testimony from families, experts, and eyewitnesses.

Sheriff Turnbull found that the crash happened because the helicopter's engines 'flamed out' due to a lack of fuel, caused by Capt Traill failing to ensure at least one fuel transfer pump switch was on.
Sheriff Turnbull said Capt Traill ignored the low fuel warnings and took a chance that they were erroneous, a conscious decision with fatal consequences.
Sheriff Turnbull said the Eurocopter EC135 should have had a visible and audible warning when both fuel transfer pumps were switched off.

Sheriff Turnbull noted it was 'surprising' that it took two years after the AAIB report to confirm no criminal proceedings, and that the Crown Office's investigation team was not sufficiently resourced.
A Crown Office spokesperson acknowledged the delay in convening the inquiry and said additional funding had been provided to recruit staff.
Airbus Helicopters expressed sadness and said it had taken immediate action to understand the root cause and noted the findings of both the AAIB and FAI.

3-17441-15-t.subevent: Italy's Economy Minister Roberto Gualtieri said on Wednesday that the main business lobby's forecast of a 6% fall in gross domestic product this year due to the coronavirus crisis is realistic.
On Tuesday national business association Confindustria said the outbreak would cause a serious recession in 2020.
Gualtieri told newspaper Il Fatto Quotidiano in an interview that the estimates are realistic and that the Italian economy can aim at a vigorous rebound.
The government is not due to give its own estimates of the impact until the end of April, when it is scheduled to publish its Document of Economy and Finance (DEF).
Italy's output rose 0.3% last year, and the government expected it to grow 0.6% this year, before the infectious disease emerged in the country at the end of February.
At the end of March, two sources told Reuters that the Treasury expected the economy to contract around 3% this year.

Gualtieri said a new stimulus package, set to be approved this month, would be 'significantly larger' than the measures worth 25 billion euros passed in March and that it would be sufficient to support companies and households for the entire length of the coronavirus epidemic.
He said it would include an extension of state-backed guarantees for companies' seeking liquidity, unemployment benefits and support to people on low incomes.

The minister also said the use of the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) to combat the crisis, under current conditions, was not an option and that, on top of the European Central Banks' intervention, Europe needed to coordinate a shared fiscal policy.
He said new solutions are needed to grant parity of conditions and to define an adequate shared and responsible response.

21-31050-3-1.subevent: Yoshiro Mori resigned as head of the Tokyo Olympics on Friday after sexist remarks he made about women.
Mori announced his resignation at a meeting of the Olympic Committee's executive board and council.
Mori had reportedly said women talk too much and have a strong sense of rivalry during a board meeting earlier this month.
Mori apologized and retracted his remarks, acknowledging they were inappropriate and against the Olympic spirit.
Mori apologized again as he announced his resignation, saying his inappropriate comments caused big trouble.
Mori said he felt his comments were misinterpreted by the media and that he was not prejudiced against women.
IOC President Thomas Bach issued a statement saying the IOC fully respects Mori's decision to step down.
The Tokyo Games organizers are trying to convince the world they can ensure a safe environment for athletes and fans amid the pandemic.
Japan extended its state of emergency in Tokyo and other regions by another month.
Japan reported its worst one-day death toll for the pandemic Thursday with 121 new deaths.
Hundreds of Olympic volunteers quit and local organizers received thousands of complaints following Mori's remarks.
Naomi Osaka called Mori's comments 'really ignorant' and Kosuke Hagino called them 'very unfortunate.'
Several sponsors voiced concerns about Mori's remarks.
A group of female opposition lawmakers wore white with roses in protest of Mori's remarks.
Japan stands 121st out of 153 countries in the World Economic Forum's 2020 gender gap index.
Koichi Nakano said the negative reaction to Mori's comments was practically unanimous.
Heather Dichter said the biggest thing people will remember about the Tokyo Games is how they dealt with the pandemic.

33-2542-7-1.subevent: Marines used a new electronic warfare system on the deck of USS Boxer to down a hostile Iranian drone during a transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS) used electronic jammers, radars, and gun systems to take out the UAV.
The encounter was the first known kill by a new generation of electronic warfare and directed energy weapons developed by the U.S.
The Navy and Marines have been concerned about swarms of cheap but lethal unmanned vehicles that could overwhelm defenses.
The Navy has tested less expensive options at sea to shoot down drones, including 5-inch deck guns and Phalanx Close-in Weapons Systems, with limited success.
In 2014, the Navy deployed a 30-kilowatt laser aboard a ship in the Persian Gulf as an early test of a directed energy weapon at sea.
The Navy is moving to install its first 60-kilowatt HELIOS directed energy weapon on a destroyer in 2021.
In January, Northrop Grumman won a contract to develop the Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program (SEWIP) Block III electronic attack capability for U.S. warships.
Callender said using systems like MADIS is less escalatory than shooting a missile and could provide deniability.

1-15230-2-1.subevent: Children in Bamyan province are helping with the potato harvest, and many young girls are also going to school for the first time.
10-year-old Hamida says she had never been to school until last year.
According to Unicef, 3.2 million girls are now getting an education in Afghanistan, a dramatic rise from 2001 when the US-led invasion ended the Taliban ban on girls' schooling.
The female literacy rate has tripled but remains around 13%, one of the world's lowest.
Gulnaz, who was raped and then charged with adultery after becoming pregnant, gave birth in jail before President Hamid Karzai granted her a pardon last year.
Women's groups have criticized Karzai for not taking a stronger stand on women's rights, accusing him of keeping his wife out of the media due to fears of conservative religious leaders.

At the Suriya school in Kabul, girls' cricket team practices under a male coach, and a UK charity, Afghan Connection, has provided equipment donated by British schools, with support from London's Marylebone Cricket Club.
A 12-year-old girl at the school says she wants to be a journalist.

Outside Kabul, changes are patchy; most Afghans live in rural areas where poverty, conflict, and conservative attitudes keep girls at home, and 60% of the 4.2 million children not in education are girls, mostly in rural and conflict-affected areas.
The Taliban have forced many schools in the conflict belt to close, and it is dangerous to be a teacher in southern Afghanistan.

Afghanistan's Education Minister Farooq Wardak insists the momentum of change will last after the US withdrawal in 2014, saying only when women feel they are 'the owner of this nation' can Afghanistan be made.
Afghan Connection has funded construction of more than 30 schools and focuses on rural areas, with Director Dr Sarah Fayne emphasizing the importance of proximity and female teachers.
Dr Sarah Fayne says she is convinced the changes of the past decade are permanent, as she can't believe people who have let their kids go to school will allow that to be taken away.

Hamida still helps at home and in the fields, but six days a week she walks 2km uphill to her local school, and her mother, who had no school in her time, hopes her daughter's dream of becoming a doctor comes true.

6-19726-1-1.subevent: France's Biomérieux has given its proprietary formula for coronavirus testing chemicals to the Canadian government for free.
In March, Canada passed emergency legislation allowing the government and third parties to produce patented goods without consent.
Biomérieux reported a 21.5% increase in sales in the first quarter, partly due to demand for reagent.
The Public Health Agency of Canada described the arrangement as a temporary license allowing the government to manufacture Biomérieux products for coronavirus testing at no cost.
PHAC said its manufacturing was still in development and testing, aiming to alleviate shortages soon.
Biomérieux's Canadian unit emailed customers in early April saying the move was meant to clear up testing backlogs and that it was boosting its own production.
Other major suppliers of RNA extraction equipment and reagents, including Thermo Fisher Scientific, Qiagen, and Roche, are facing soaring demand.
Biomérieux said in its customer note that it hoped the move would allow federal and provincial labs to test more Canadians and reduce testing backlogs.
On Thursday, Canada pledged C$1.1 billion for research and drug or vaccine manufacturing in its fight against the coronavirus.

1-14903-2-2.subevent: Chile has seen looting, arson, attacks on police stations and vehicles, and destruction of an ambulance amid daily protests that often end in clashes with security forces.

President Sebastian Pinera addressed the nation, saying he was sending an urgent bill to Congress to allow the army to safeguard key installations and police stations without declaring a state of emergency.
The government said about one-third of the estimated $1.5bn worth of destruction since protests began on October 18 was caused by criminal gangs, common criminals, drug traffickers, and anarchists.
Graffiti in Santiago expressed anger, with messages like 'Accumulate fury,' 'keep going until dignity becomes normal,' and 'make the cuicos (the rich) shiver.'
A protester named Mario, a 25-year-old who had just lost his job as an assistant accountant, said peaceful protests for 30 years had achieved nothing and that violence was needed to force change.

Maria, a 23-year-old protester, said the rich and powerful threw the first stone by discriminating and leaving them without education and healthcare, and that destroying a bus or throwing stones was less violent.
Maria Olga, a professional from an upper-middle-class neighborhood, said she didn't recognize her country and that those causing destruction couldn't be Chileans.
Maria and Mario described themselves as 'radical opponents of the system' but said they had no political affiliation and were not asking for jewels or gold, only decent income and basic services.
A new study showed that 58 percent of Chileans belong to the lower-middle-class or 'vulnerable class' who cannot access basic needs under the current system.
Mario expressed deep distrust of political institutions and said he didn't believe in voting because he felt unrepresented by any party.

0-4407-1-1.subevent: A double-decker bus overturned into a field in Devon on Saturday 5 October.
Emergency services declared a 'major incident' after the crash on the A385 between Totnes and Paignton at around 11am.
Emergency services adopted a multi-agency approach and deployed a large number of police, fire and ambulance vehicles.
Numerous air ambulances attended the scene.
Devon and Cornwall Police released a statement at 5:30pm saying 37 people sustained injuries, with eight described as having potentially serious injuries.
The force confirmed the road will close again from 7am on Sunday 6 October while emergency crews recover the bus from the field.
The force added that there's significant pressure on local health services as a result of the crash.
People were urged not to attend A&E departments in the area unless it's a real emergency.

1-14955-1-t.subevent: President Trump pointed to a bar chart in a news briefing showing Belgium's coronavirus death toll per capita as the highest among countries.
Belgian government minister Denis Ducarme called Trump's display 'macabre' and 'level zero' politics.
Ducarme tweeted that Belgium's method of counting COVID-19 deaths is the most exhaustive possible.
Belgian authorities decided to include both confirmed and suspected COVID-19 deaths in their national tally.
As of Wednesday, Belgium counted 6,262 deaths from COVID-19, with more than half in nursing homes.
Belgian authorities came under pressure to change their counting method due to negative perception.
Prime Minister Sophie Wilmès suggested the count has been exaggerated.
Emmanuel André, spokesman for the government's coronavirus task force, insisted other governments have been undercounting fatalities.
Experts said Belgium likely hit the coronavirus peak on April 12.
A special task force is due to unveil a gradual exit strategy from lockdown measures on Friday.

7-36661-5-2.subevent: The Technical University of Denmark (DTU) has been shut down, but Professor Anders Wolff continues working on the CoronaDX project.
Project partner Professor Anders Fomsgaard from Statens Seruminstitut also continues working because two of the three instruments are scheduled to be ready for emergency use in October.
The third instrument is scheduled to be ready in March 2021.
Several research teams are working on a vaccine, but it will be 1-2 years at best before it is approved for use.
The fastest instrument will give the diagnosis in less than one minute, and the slowest in less than an hour.
All three instruments are being designed to be very easy to use, like a pregnancy test, for use in clinics or at home.
Professor Anders Fomsgaard is responsible for the development of two of the instruments, including the fastest one.
Professor Anders Wolff says the project is developing unusually fast because researchers are working together rather than as competitors.
The three new instruments measure in three different ways to recognize the virus, and the technology was recently developed in another EU funded project for detecting poultry diseases.
As early as June, two Chinese partners will test two of the instruments in the field in China.

2-35026-1-t.subevent: France seized a British scallop dredger, the Cornelis Gert Jan, in French waters and escorted it to Le Havre after its crew failed to prove it was allowed to fish there.
A second British vessel was given a verbal warning by French authorities.
France listed potential sanctions against Britain if there is no progress in talks, including extra customs checks on British goods from Nov. 2 and a threat to cut electricity exports.
French Seas Minister Annick Girardin said 'It's not war, but it is a fight' regarding the dispute.
The British government called the French reaction 'disappointing and disproportionate'.

Environment minister George Eustice challenged France's statement that the boat had no license and said the threatened steps appeared incompatible with the post-Brexit trade deal and international law.
Eustice warned that if France carried through with the steps, they would be met with an 'appropriate and calibrated response'.
European Affairs Minister Clement Beaune said France needed to speak the language of strength because that's what the British government understands.
Girardin said France could not cut off electricity supplies but could raise tariffs.
The Cornelis Gert Jan's skipper was placed under preliminary investigation for dredging 2,160 kg of scallops and could face a 75,000-euro fine.
The vessel's owners said it had a fishing license and had been fishing legally, with a director calling it a 'pawn of bigger forces'.
Barrie Deas, head of Britain's National Federation of Fishermen's Organisations, said France appeared determined to escalate the license row before a presidential election.
Bruno Margolle, head of the Boulogne fishermen's collective, said 15 of 37 license requests from his region previously shown as rejected had passed to 'under consideration' since the boat was held.
In Le Havre, scallop fishermen expressed frustration with British vessels' access to shellfish, with Pascal Coquet saying 'There has to be an end to this fraud'.

0-4882-1-2.subevent: The Air Force's X-37B Orbital Test Vehicle Mission 5 successfully landed at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Shuttle Landing Facility on Oct. 27, 2019, at 3:51 a.m.
The spaceplane conducted on-orbit experiments for 780 days, breaking its own record by being in orbit for more than two years.

Secretary of the Air Force Barbara Barrett stated that the X-37B continues to demonstrate the importance of a reusable spaceplane and that each successive mission advances the nation's space capabilities.
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David L. Goldfein said the safe return of the spacecraft after breaking its endurance record is the result of an innovative partnership between government and industry.

Randy Walden, Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office director, said the X-37B completed its longest flight to date and successfully completed all mission objectives, hosting Air Force Research Laboratory experiments and providing a ride for small satellites.

Lt. Col. Jonathan Keen, X-37B program manager, said the spacecraft is a key component of the space community and the milestone demonstrates commitment to conducting experiments for America's future space exploration.
The X-37B landed at the Kennedy Space Center Shuttle Landing Facility for the second time, with Mission 4 having landed after 718 days in orbit.
Brig. Gen. Doug Schiess, 45th Space Wing commander, said the team had been preparing for the event and he was proud of their hard work and dedication culminating in the safe and successful landing.

The fifth mission launched on Sept. 7, 2017, from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 booster, and the Air Force is preparing to launch the sixth X-37B mission from CCAFS in 2020.

9-21348-5-1.subevent: The article describes the reasons Central Americans leave their homes, including killings, gang recruitment, rape, police harassment, and death threats.

The U.S. saw record numbers of migrant apprehensions along its border with Mexico in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Today's migrant flow includes more families, newborns, children, and pregnant women escaping life-or-death situations, not just male heads of household.

In 1996, U.S. authorities approved the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, leading to deportations of convicted criminals to Central America and the expansion of gangs like MS-13 and Barrio 18.
The region's civil wars, inequality, mass incarceration, and weak institutions created today's gang problem, with gangs taking over rural and urban areas.
Parents in gang-plagued 'red zones' spend money on private transport or after-school programs to protect their children from gangs.
In El Salvador, boys as young as 12 are targeted for gang recruitment, and girls may be sexually abused or forced into gang membership.
Gang recruitment is gradual, starting with gifts or invitations to parties, and families who refuse to leave are threatened.
Despite prevention efforts, gangs remain undefeated and have penetrated the social fabric, with officials admitting they are 'fighting a war they cannot win.'
Governments rely on security crackdowns, which create fear of police and counter-productive impacts in communities.
Thousands of Central American families are forced to flee despite dangerous journeys, as they face life-or-death situations at home.
Displaced people say U.S. migration policies make them anxious, but there is no scarier place than their home countries.
A friend from Guatemala said people are willing to risk the journey because it's a life or death situation.

0-4546-1-2.subevent: Three people died after a quick-moving wildfire churned through the foothills of Southern California.
Evacuation orders were lifted in all of Los Angeles County and in parts of Riverside County.
The Saddleridge Fire ignited late Thursday in Sylmar, destroying more than 30 structures.

Garcetti tweeted an image of him signing paperwork to ensure agencies take necessary steps to protect lives and property.

Jacob Margolis described the scene from a staging area at Hansen Dam.

SoCalGas tweeted that there were no indications of damage or leaks at the Aliso Canyon facility.

1-15178-2-1.subevent: Portugal's Catholic bishops announced the suspension of public Masses from Saturday due to the 'extreme gravity' of the coronavirus crisis.
The bishops stated that it is a moral imperative for all citizens, particularly Christians, to take maximum sanitary precautions to avoid contagion.
Portugal recorded 609,000 COVID-19 cases and 9,920 deaths as of Jan. 22.
This was the second time the bishops suspended public worship, the first being in March 2020, with restrictions eased at the end of May.
The bishops said public Masses, catechesis, and other pastoral activities requiring gatherings would be suspended from Jan. 23, and they called on priests to offer livestreamed Masses.
Earlier in January, the bishops had called for the suspension or postponement of baptisms, confirmations, and marriages.
The bishops said funerals could be celebrated according to norms issued in May last year, requiring social distance.

The Shrine of Our Lady of Fatima announced it would broadcast three Masses and two rosary prayers daily while public Masses are suspended.
Shrine rector Fr. Carlos Cabecinhas said that while it is not the same to be physically present, following via television is the one possible way to participate now.

1-14989-2-3.subevent: A new study found that the megatooth shark Otodus megalodon was the largest shark to ever swim in Earth's oceans.
O. megalodon lived approximately 23 to 3.6 million years ago, and the exact cause of its extinction is still debated.
A recent study in Scientific Reports concluded that a full-grown O. megalodon could reach about 50 feet (15 meters) in length.
A new study in Historical Biology, led by Kenshu Shimada, compiled a database of 70 shark species and inferred their sizes from fossil records.
The study used measurements from 13 present-day non-planktivorous sharks to generate functions relating teeth dimensions, jaw length, and body size, then applied them to fossil teeth.
The study showed that non-planktivorous sharks have a general size limit of 23 feet (7 meters), while some plankton-eating sharks can reach 26 to 32 feet (8 to 10 meters).
The study also showed that sharks got on average bigger in the last 65 million years, but O. megalodon, at 46 to 50 feet, was exceptionally large.
The study noted that warm-bloodedness and oophagy have been proposed as adaptations enabling shark gigantism.
Based on growth models, a newborn megalodon was already 9 feet (3 meters) long.

10-6887-1-2.subevent: Dozens of climate activists invaded BlackRock's office in central Paris on Monday.
The activists called for the fund to pull out of fossil fuel investments.
Green activists from Extinction Rebellion and Fridays for Future managed to enter the building and reach the fourth floor, where they graffitied walls.
Emilia, a 15-year-old Fridays for Future group member, said they were trying to convey what they are asking for and want to change the capitalistic system.

BlackRock Chief Executive Larry Fink warned company boards in January to step up efforts to tackle climate change or face increased wrath from investors.

Extinction Rebellion last month targeted Royal Dutch Shell's headquarters in The Hague and McKinsey & Co's London office, and staged a demonstration at a Brussels car show at which 185 protesters were detained.

11-23153-1-1.subevent: Zanzibar's first Vice President and ACT Wazalendo's Chairman Maalim Seif Sharif Hamad died at the age of 77.

1-15800-4-1.subevent: Tropical Depression 5 strengthened into Tropical Storm Edouard at 11 p.m. EDT on July 5 (0300 UTC, July 6).
On July 6 at 1:45 a.m. EDT, NASA's Aqua satellite analyzed Edouard's cloud tops in infrared light.
The MODIS instrument found a small area of powerful thunderstorms northeast of the center with cloud top temperatures as cold as or colder than minus 70 degrees Fahrenheit.
Southwesterly wind shear was pushing the strongest storms northeast of the center, leaving the rest of Edouard as an exposed swirl of low- to mid-level clouds.
At 5 a.m. EDT on July 6, Edouard was centered about 530 miles south of Cape Race, Newfoundland, with maximum sustained winds near 40 mph and an estimated minimum central pressure of 1008 millibars.
Edouard was moving toward the northeast near 36 mph, with this motion expected to continue for the next couple of days as it tracks toward the United Kingdom.

National Hurricane Center forecaster Jack Beven noted that the cyclone is in strong southwesterly wind shear, heading for colder water, and approaching a frontal system, which should lead to extratropical transition in 12 to 24 hours.
Beven also noted that after transition, the extratropical low should persist for another 24 hours or so before dissipating.

0-4813-2.subevent: A report found that a series of failures led to the crash of a Lion Air flight, which killed 189 people and led to the grounding of the Boeing 737 Max.
Investigators said faults by Boeing, Lion Air and pilots caused the crash.
Five months after the disaster, an Ethiopian Airlines plane crashed, killing all 157 people on board, which led to the grounding of the entire 737 Max fleet.
On Friday, air crash investigators in Indonesia released their final report, detailing the list of events that caused the Lion Air jet to plunge into the Java Sea.

The report found that the jet should have been grounded before departing on the fatal flight because of an earlier cockpit issue, but the issue was not recorded properly and the plane was allowed to take off without the fault being fixed.
The report found that a crucial sensor, bought from a repair shop in Florida, had not been properly tested, and on Friday the US aviation regulator revoked the company's certification.

0-4716-1-2.subevent: The social uprising in Chile has reached its fourth month, with masses of people continuing to protest and demand structural change despite ferocious repression by the militarized Carabineros police force.

Two months before the scheduled plebiscite, the answer remains uncertain, with approval ratings of Chile's institutions at an all-time low.
Protesters expressed hopes for ending the neoliberal system and the Pinochet Constitution, and fears that nothing will change.
The month of March is deemed definitive in the struggle, as Chileans return to daily life and continue to demand a new political and socioeconomic model.

0-4472-6-1.subevent: Ecuador's election halted Latin America's shift to the right.

2-34752-6-2.subevent: Harmful algae usually bloom during the warm summer season or when water temperatures are warmer than usual.

Climate change might lead to more droughts, which make freshwater saltier, causing marine algae to invade freshwater ecosystems.
In the southwestern and south central United States, toxic marine algae have been killing fish in freshwater lakes since 2000.
Higher levels of carbon dioxide in the air and water can lead to rapid growth of algae, especially toxic blue-green algae that can float to the surface of the water.
Climate change might affect rainfall patterns, leading to alternating periods of drought and intense storms, which can cause more nutrient runoff into waterbodies, feeding more algal blooms.
Scientists predict that sea level could rise up to one meter by the year 2100, creating more shallow and stable coastal water, conditions that are perfect for the growth of algae.

Climate change is expected to alter the timing and intensity of coastal upwelling, and along the west coast of the United States, excess nutrients delivered by upwelling might lead to more algal blooms.

1-15885-8-t.subevent: The global effort to secure a COVID-19 vaccine through the COVAX facility has been set in motion.

On Jan. 10, 2020, SARS-CoV-2 sequence data was shared through the GISAID Initiative.

The pharmaceutical industry's commitment to develop, manufacture, and make vaccines available stems from the belief that no one is safe unless everyone is safe from COVID-19.

16-10208-2-1.subevent: Die Stadt Mönchengladbach teilte am Dienstagvormittag mit, dass Borussia und der 1. FC Köln am Mittwochabend ohne Zuschauer spielen müssen.

2-34832-7-t.subevent: Coca and poppy cultivation in the Andean jungle is significantly damaging the environment through deforestation, soil erosion, and chemical pollution.

Archaeologists have discovered artifacts indicating coca leaf chewing was used from Chile to Central America since 2100 BC.

Coca evolved into a cash crop over the last century, from commercial and medicinal uses to a multi-billion dollar drug business.
During a fifteen-year period beginning in the 1970s, 700,000 hectares of rain forest in the Amazon basin were destroyed to clear land for coca growth.
Farmers place coca and poppy fields on hillsides to avoid government eradication, and rarely employ soil conservation techniques, leading to severe soil erosion.
Topsoil runoff from eroded fields fills waterways, changes river courses, causes flooding, and kills fish and aquatic plant life.
Pollution from insecticides, fertilizers, and processing chemicals also contributes to environmental damage.

12-wiki-img/8436-1/8436-1-2.subevent: The University of Manitoba is using anti-cheating software that records students' webcams during some remote exams.

9-21751-1-2.subevent: Clashes broke out Sunday morning in three cities across Israel as police attempted to enforce coronavirus lockdown restrictions in ultra-Orthodox communities.

0-4560-1-1JPG.subevent: A court in Ecuador ordered the arrest of former president Rafael Correa over his alleged involvement in the 2012 kidnapping of an opponent.
Judge Daniella Camacho said she has alerted Interpol to have the 55-year-old Correa extradited.
Former lawmaker Fernando Balda was briefly kidnapped in Bogotá, Colombia, where he fled during escalating tensions with Correa.
Balda accuses Correa of masterminding the abduction.
The judge said Correa had failed to comply with an order to appear in court in Quito to assist with the investigation.
Correa instead presented himself to the Ecuadorean consulate in Brussels, which the judge said was a violation of her orders.

Correa accuses current president Lenín Moreno of conducting a smear campaign against him.
Correa's lawyer Caupolican Ochoa said the decision was arbitrary and defamatory, resulting from political pressure, and that he would appeal.
Arrest warrants have been issued for three police intelligence agents, an ex-police commander, and a former top intelligence official, who was arrested in Spain last month.

9-21751-1-3.subevent: Clashes broke out Sunday morning in three cities across Israel as police attempted to enforce coronavirus lockdown restrictions in ultra-Orthodox communities.

In Jerusalem's Mea Shearim neighborhood, hundreds of people clashed with police attempting to shut down a yeshiva that had opened illegally, with police surrounded by a crowd shouting insults and throwing trash.
Police arrested one person in Mea Shearim and later brought in water cannon trucks to disperse the crowd.

In Ashdod, police were confronted while closing down an ultra-Orthodox elementary school that had opened despite rules, with several dozen people trying to force their way into the compound, injuring four officers and causing damage.
Protesters in Ashdod blocked traffic and confronted police, leading to four arrests.

In Bnei Brak, clashes broke out as police tried to shut down schools linked to the Vizhnitz Hasidic dynasty, whose head rabbi had ruled that educational institutions should open before apparently backtracking.

Last week, clashes broke out in Bnei Brak after a mob injured a police officer, with at least six people arrested; the rioters belonged to an extremist faction of the Vizhnitz Hasidic sect.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the Friday attack in Bnei Brak, stating that lawbreakers would be dealt with heavily.

1-15205-8-t.subevent: Bridgett Floyd, sister of George Floyd, urged protesters to 'be his legacy' at a rally in Washington DC.
Relatives of black Americans harmed or killed by police addressed the event, including Jacob Blake Sr, who said the verdict on racism in America was 'guilty, guilty, guilty!'.
Thousands gathered in Washington DC for the Commitment March: Get Your Knee Off Our Necks, commemorating the 1963 March on Washington and protesting police violence.
The event was organized by Reverend Al Sharpton and Martin Luther King III, and brought together generations of activists to call for police reform and urge Americans to vote.
Speakers demanded racial justice and urged people to vote, with many calling for passage of the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act.
Attendees lined Constitution Avenue as early as 7am, with some expressing urgency about the crisis of police violence against African-Americans.

Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley paid tribute to black Americans' activism, and Senator Kamala Harris addressed the rally virtually, urging marchers to 'march on for our ancestors and for our children and grandchildren'.
Organizers said the agenda included slavery reparations, defunding police departments, and investment in healthcare, housing, and social services in black communities.

25-4120-1-t.subevent: Ten people were arrested during a climate change protest in Dover aimed at blockading the port.
Four of the arrested, including men in their 80s and 90s, staged a sit-in at the Eastern Docks Roundabout.
Extinction Rebellion campaigners legally occupied part of the A20, off the roundabout, near the port.
The campaign group said the 'No Food on a Dying Planet' protest centered around potential food shortages as climate change develops.
Kent Police set up a designated area on the westbound A20 for activists to demonstrate to minimize disruption.
Some protesters blockaded part of the A2 by gluing themselves to the road and were removed by police.
One protester who had glued their hands to the road was taken away on a stretcher.
Ch Supt Andy Pritchard said disruption was kept to a minimum.
Live music was expected later as part of the demonstration, with flags and signs adorning seafront railings.
The protest was due to last until 15:00 BST.
The protest came a day after thousands of people across the UK took part in a global 'climate strike day'.
Chris Atkins from Extinction Rebellion Dover said that as climate change develops, millions of ordinary Britons will face the real and growing threat of food shortages, hunger, and starvation.
A Port of Dover spokeswoman said it was experiencing intermittent delays due to the protest and was working with Kent Police to ensure minimal disruption.

3-16947-3-t.subevent: ENEA announced that one of Italy's most powerful supercomputers, CRESCO6, will be made available to public and private scientific research against the coronavirus.
The CRESCO6 infrastructure, located at the ENEA Center in Portici near Naples, can perform up to 1.4 million billion mathematical operations per second.
ENEA President Federico Testa stated that the supercomputer can provide a vital contribution to the search for drugs, vaccines, and data processing in this crucial moment for Italy.

Testa added that CRESCO6 is already available to a team of researchers from the University of Florence, coordinated by Professor Piero Procacci, who are working on a process to block the replication mechanism of COVID-19 at its root.

ENEA reported that HPC CRESCO6 is the second most important public computing infrastructure in Italy after Cineca and is playing a key role in testing the effectiveness of compounds under investigation, providing reliable predictions of inhibitory efficacy in a few hours based on atomistic simulations on thousands of parallel processors.
Within a few days of testing with Professor Procacci's team, at least two compounds with promising characteristics were identified, one of which is commercially available.
After the initial phase of structural refinement of the compounds, HPC CRESCO6 will be used to try to identify the optimal molecular structure for a possible specific antiviral drug for COVID-19.
Since 2018, CRESCO6 has been listed in the prestigious TOP500 ranking of the world's top 500 supercomputers, after its power was doubled to 1.4 petaflops.
The entry at 420th place was announced at SuperComputing 2018 in Dallas, the main conference in the field of scientific computing.
ENEA invited researchers from public and private institutions to submit requests to use its computational resources by writing to crescoforcovid19@enea.it.

7-36258-7-2.subevent: Medical equipment, such as a mobile ultrasound vehicle and a mobile X-ray vehicle, were seen at Singapore Expo on Friday (April 10), as preparations were made for the facility to receive its first batch of Covid-19 patients.
Close to 20 people were seen alighting from two minibuses outside the Expo on Friday night.
This first batch of patients are either recovering or have mild symptoms.
Singapore Expo is the Republic's second community isolation facility.
One hall will house patients in recovery while those with a mild case of the coronavirus will be treated in the other.

Since last month, recovering Covid-19 patients have been transferred from the National Centre for Infectious Diseases to private hospitals, as well as Singapore's first community isolation facility, D'Resort NTUC.

0-4654-1-t.subevent: The New York State Department of Health announced new findings of its ongoing investigation into vaping-associated pulmonary illnesses, including an updated case count and information about testing at the Wadsworth Center Laboratory.
Health Commissioner Dr. Howard Zucker urged the public to be vigilant about vaping products and to contact health care providers if they develop unusual symptoms.
The Department issued a health advisory in August alerting health care providers of the emerging health threat and listing symptoms to look for.

As of September 5, 2019, the Department received 34 reports from physicians of severe pulmonary illness among patients aged 15 to 46 who used at least one cannabis-containing vape product before becoming ill.

Laboratory test results showed very high levels of vitamin E acetate in nearly all cannabis-containing samples analyzed, and at least one vitamin E acetate containing vape product was linked to each patient who submitted a product for testing.
Vitamin E acetate became a key focus of the investigation, and the Department continued to investigate its health effects when inhaled.

The Wadsworth Center tested both cannabis and nicotine-containing vape products, including more than a dozen product samples from patients, for a range of substances including THC, nicotine, synthetic cannabinoids, opioids, and pesticides.
The Department advised people not certified in the Medical Marijuana Program to consider not using any vape products, and warned against using unregulated products purchased off the street.

The Department advised anyone experiencing symptoms who uses vape products to contact their healthcare provider immediately, and healthcare providers to report possible cases to the local poison control center.

0-4857-5-2.subevent: California faces a critical fire danger Thursday morning as at least a half dozen wildfires burn across the state.
Forecasters say high winds and low humidity are increasing the risk of wildfires.
PG&E preemptively shut off electricity to more than 700,000 customers due to weather conditions.
Resident Ron Blasingame said he regrets not buying a generator and criticized PG&E for not clearing brush from its lines.
Many residents waited in long lines to fill their gas tanks before the pumps lost electricity and shut down.
Barry Friedman's home improvement store lost power, but he kept it open by guiding customers by flashlight to purchase goods.
Debbie Medina, who relies on a CPAP machine and oxygen generators, said her condition prevents her from getting to community centers.
PG&E said putting existing overhead lines in fire threat areas underground could cost as much as $110 billion.

1-15310-1-t.subevent: A migrant boat sank off Tunisia on Sunday, killing at least 11 African migrants.
Tunisia's coast guard recovered the bodies of eight women and three children off the coast near Sfax.
About 30 people had set out on the boat, aiming to reach Italy.
The coast guard is searching for the other missing people.
Last year, about 90 African migrants drowned after their boat capsized en route to Europe from Libya.

1-14979-1-1.subevent: The Nobel Committee in Physics honored Charles Kao, Willard S. Boyle, and George E. Smith as 'masters of light'.
Kao's discoveries led to the widespread use of fiber optics.
Boyle and Smith invented the charge-coupled device, which captures light in digital cameras.
Boyle and Smith initially wanted to construct novel electronic memory rather than an imaging device.
The article notes that the Nobel Committee has previously awarded prizes for discoveries made much earlier than the preceding year.
The time from initial discovery to Nobel acknowledgment has generally increased since the first prize in 1901.
The committee may have wanted to avoid controversies like the 1938 award to Enrico Fermi, whose discovery was disproved the following year.
The article concludes that the spirit of Nobel's intention remains intact, as the winners have made a fundamental impact on the world.

1-14991-2-2.subevent: Researchers identified 24 exoplanets outside our solar system that may have conditions more suitable for life than Earth.

A study led by Dirk Schulze-Makuch published in the journal Astrobiology detailed characteristics of potential superhabitable planets, including those that are older, larger, warmer, and wetter than Earth.
The 24 top contenders are all more than 100 light years away, and the study could help focus future observation efforts by telescopes like NASA's James Webb Space Telescope.
Schulze-Makuch stated that it is important to select targets for upcoming space telescopes and to not get stuck looking for a second Earth.
Schulze-Makuch teamed up with astronomers Rene Heller and Edward Guinan to identify superhabitability criteria and search among 4,500 known exoplanets.
The researchers selected planet-star systems with probable terrestrial planets in the habitable zone from the Kepler Object of Interest Exoplanet Archive.
The researchers looked at systems with K dwarf stars, which have longer lifespans, allowing planets to be older and giving life more time to advance.
The researchers argued that the sweet spot for life is a planet between 5 billion to 8 billion years old, and that a planet 10% larger and 1.5 times Earth's mass would be more habitable.
The authors argued that a slightly warmer temperature and more moisture would be better for life, as seen in tropical rainforests.
Among the 24 top planet candidates, none meet all criteria for superhabitable planets, but one has four critical characteristics.

6-18762-1-1.subevent: France's Biomérieux gave its proprietary formula for coronavirus testing chemicals to the Canadian government for free.
Canada passed emergency legislation in March giving the government and third parties the right to produce patented goods without consent.
Biomérieux reported a 21.5% increase in sales in the first quarter, partly due to demand for reagent.
The Public Health Agency of Canada described the arrangement as a temporary license allowing the government to manufacture Biomérieux products for coronavirus testing.
PHAC said its manufacturing was still in development and testing, aiming to alleviate shortages soon.
Biomérieux's Canadian unit emailed customers in early April saying the move was meant to clear up testing backlogs.
The company said it was also boosting its own production.
Biomérieux said in its customer note that it hoped the move would allow federal and provincial labs to test more Canadians and reduce testing backlogs.
On Thursday, Canada pledged C$1.1 billion for research and drug or vaccine manufacturing in its fight against the coronavirus.

0-4491-3-3.subevent: The Obama administration issued sanctions against Maduro's administration in 2015 on grounds of human rights violations.
On Monday, the US government imposed fresh sanctions against Venezuela's national oil firm, PDVSA, to freeze exchanges and block imports.
Venezuela's power crisis escalated on Jan. 23 when opposition leader Juan Guaidó invoked a constitutional right to take presidential powers and call for new elections.
Numerous nations in Latin America, Europe, and Canada deemed Maduro's 2018 election victory illegitimate and recognized Guaidó's legitimacy.
On Monday, Guaidó asked congress to appoint new board members to PDVSA just before the US issued fresh sanctions.
US national security adviser John Bolton said sanctions would block $7 billion in PDVSA's assets plus over $11 billion in lost export proceeds over the next year.
David Smolansky, former mayor of El Hatillo, said the sanctions have debilitated high officials' ability to move internationally and their financial possibilities abroad.
Rafael Uzcátegui, director of Provea, lamented the sanctions, saying they could limit transactions Maduro's government could make to import food and medicine.
In 2017, Venezuela's Supreme Court nullified the opposition-led National Assembly, leading to months of protests with over 160 deaths.
The Trump administration imposed new sanctions against Venezuela in 2017, and Maduro accused the US of plunging Venezuelan citizens further into economic crisis.
By 2018, the US expanded sanctions to include First Lady Cilia Flores and Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees reported that more than 3 million Venezuelans had fled the country since 2014.
The Venezuelan Observatory of Health highlighted that 94 percent of Venezuelans don't have enough revenue to pay for basic supplies.
Venezuelan prisons and intelligence services hold more than 230 political prisoners and have arrested more than 12,500 people since 2014, according to Foro Penal.
Human Rights Watch denounced police and armed forces for abuses, saying some amount to torture.
A 2019 report by Provea estimates 250 people have been killed in protests during the Maduro era.
On Jan. 30, thousands marched in Caracas calling for the end of Maduro.
The latest sanctions halt all US oil purchases in an attempt to support Guaidó and push Maduro out of power.

0-4399-3-1.subevent: Federal authorities revealed that active Russian cyberattacks are targeting a wide swath of American government networks, including those involved with the ongoing election.

The FBI and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a bulletin stating that the Russian hacking group Energetic Bear or FireFly is targeting U.S. state, local, territorial, and tribal government networks, as well as aviation networks.
U.S. officials said that systems in two local government jurisdictions had been accessed, granting attackers admission to some limited data about voters.

Chris Krebs, director of CISA, said at a briefing that the attackers were opportunistic and used vulnerabilities in county government infrastructures to move within offices, leading them to some publicly available voting data in at least one case.
The Washington Post reported that the counties breached are in California and Indiana.
Krebs said it's possible the group has breached more governments but they haven't been discovered yet.

The announcement came one day after an in-person briefing by Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe and FBI Director Christopher Wray in which they warned about Russian interference and an Iranian scheme to intimidate voters with spoof emails.
Wray said Wednesday that election infrastructure remains resilient and urged confidence that votes count, advising skepticism of early unverified claims to the contrary.
The Treasury Department announced it has sanctioned a number of Iranian government entities in connection with what U.S. officials called their interference in the election.

25-3857-2-t.subevent: Wikipedia users in Germany encountered an error message when trying to visit the online encyclopedia on Friday.
The website fell victim to a massive and widespread denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that paralyzed the site on Friday evening across Germany and other parts of Europe.
The website reappeared shortly before midnight before going offline again early Saturday.
Later Friday evening, Wikipedia tweeted that it was continuing to work on restoring access.
Social media users shared their Wikipedia woes on Twitter using the hashtag #WikipediaDown.

1-16438-6-t.subevent: WFSA is working with its global membership to curate, share and disseminate up-to-date and practical COVID-19 guidance for anaesthesia and perioperative care providers.

WFSA issued a statement on health care providers safety and wellbeing during the COVID-19 pandemic.

WFSA member societies, including the Indian Society of Anaesthesiologists and the South African Society of Anaesthesiologists, issued advisories and guidelines.
Resources in French, Spanish, and Portuguese were compiled from various organizations.
General information on COVID-19 was provided by WHO, CDC, MSF, and other sources, including training and learning resources.

1-14823-1-1.subevent: The European Union and UK have set out negotiating mandates for talks, with fisheries being a major point of divergence.
The UK's negotiating mandate, published on Thursday, differs significantly from the European Commission's proposals for managing wild fish stocks.
The fishing industry represents less than 1% of the UK economy but is of totemic importance to coastal communities and governments.

On Wednesday, Fergus Ewing, Scotland's cabinet secretary for fisheries, set out measures to improve inshore fleet operations and highlighted the sector's significance, including that 80% of Scotland's 2,000 registered fishing vessels operate in inshore waters.
The fishing industry fears that health certificates and bottlenecks at Channel ports will add delay and cost to exports of fresh or live catch to continental markets.
On Tuesday, Michel Barnier, the EU's chief negotiator, placed fisheries in the context of the free trade deal, emphasizing the need to uphold existing reciprocal access conditions and quota shares.
The EU's negotiating mandate proposes that quota shares should only be adjustable with consent from both the UK and EU, and wants joint control and inspection.
Both sides agree on the need to reach a deal by summer so that a new system for negotiating annual catch quotas can be in place before the traditional pre-Christmas negotiations.
The UK government's proposal includes annual negotiations similar to those with Norway, rejection of 'relative stability', and a focus on 'zonal attachment'.
The UK government recognizes the interests of devolved administrations in fisheries and is committed to working with them in considering any agreement.

27-33401-5-2.subevent: Pangkogabwilhan II Marsdya TNI Imran Baidirus conducted a working visit to the Poso area to survey the situation from the air as part of Operation Tinombala 2020 on Tuesday (29/12/2020).
