WFSA draws attention to the importance of appropriate precautions when providing respiratory care and intubation for patients with COVID-19.
WFSA issued a statement on health care providers safety and wellbeing during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Various organizations published guidance on anaesthesia and COVID-19, including APSF, ASA, IARS, Anesthesia & Analgesia, and others.
Guidance on airway management was provided by SIAARTI, Prince of Wales Hospital Hong Kong, and UCSF.
Guidance on obstetric anaesthesia was provided by SOAP, RCOG, and other organizations.
WFSA curated guidance for low resource settings for anesthesia providers.
WFSA member societies issued advisories and guidelines, including the Indian Society of Anaesthesiologists and the South African Society of Anaesthesiologists.
French, Spanish, and Portuguese resources were compiled from various organizations.
General information on coronavirus was provided by WHO, CDC, MSF, and others.

0-4799-1-t.subevent: Chicago Public Schools canceled classes for Thursday, the sixth day without school, as teachers remain on strike.
CPS said that as of 4 p.m., the CTU had not scheduled a House of Delegates vote to end the strike, making it impossible to hold classes on Thursday.
Chicago teachers and school employees marched downtown Wednesday, converging on a rally outside Mayor Lori Lightfoot's first city budget address.
Thousands of people marched from multiple locations into the Loop, causing rolling street closures during the morning rush hour.
Groups from four meet-up spots marched to City Hall as Lightfoot was about to address the City Council.
The Chicago Teachers Union said the event was picket lines shifting into the Loop in a joint effort with SEIU Local 73 and allied organizations.
CTU President Jesse Sharkey said, 'The city is not done hearing us yet. Together, we're going to win.'
Lightfoot delivered her budget address, unveiling proposals to help fill an $838 million budget gap, including potential tax increases.
The march and rally shifted to a sit-in on city streets as Lightfoot's address began.
Negotiations continued between the two sides in the teachers strike, which caused its fifth day of canceled classes on Wednesday.
Lightfoot said, 'There has to be a commitment and a will and a sense of urgency on all sides. That's what's going to make a difference.'
The city said its latest proposals add up to an additional $500 million more in spending for teachers and their classrooms over the next five years.
Union officials said there was a 'good conversation' between the sides on Tuesday, but they have not landed on 'just terms' in negotiations.

CTU Chief of Staff Jennifer Johnson said, 'We understand that we're not going to solve all problems, but we need to see a substantial down payment and then a plan to address class sizes and other issues.'

21-29964-7-t.subevent: LGBT campaigners in Georgia canceled a planned Pride march after opponents attacked activists and journalists and the government and church spoke out against the event.
Hundreds of violent counterprotesters took to the streets of Tbilisi against the Pride march scheduled for the evening.
At least 50 journalists were attacked by mobs at different locations, including two RFE/RL reporters.
Videos showed anti-LGBT groups waving Georgian flags scaling the Tbilisi Pride headquarters, tearing down rainbow flags, and ransacking the office.
Tbilisi Pride accused the government and church of emboldening a 'huge wave of hate' against the LGBT community and failing to protect citizens' rights.
RFE/RL President Jamie Fly condemned the attacks on journalists and demanded that Georgian authorities investigate and bring justice.
Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili said it was inappropriate to hold a Pride march, arguing it would create confrontation and was 'unacceptable for a large segment of the Georgian society.'
The Georgian Orthodox Church called on supporters to gather against the Pride march, and videos showed some priests joining the protests.
After the march was canceled, priests chanted and people danced to Georgian folk songs in front of the parliament building.
Tbilisi Pride organizers said they would continue to advocate for LGBT rights despite the violence and resistance.

The U.S. and EU diplomatic missions in Georgia, along with embassies of 16 other countries, issued a joint statement condemning the violence and calling on the government to protect peaceful assembly.
Rights groups condemned the violence and accused the government of supporting hate groups.

9-21858-2-t.subevent: Religious festivals could be cancelled or curtailed in the coming weeks because of the coronavirus crisis.
Next month, most of the world's major religions have festivals involving large gatherings of people, including Easter, Passover, Rama Navami, Vaisakhi, and Ramadan.
The traditional Easter mass at the Basilica in Rome and the pope's Urbi et Orbi blessing are in doubt after the square was closed off by Italian police and public masses and funerals were cancelled.
The Vatican is livestreaming the pope's daily mass and the Angelus, and Pope Francis has urged priests to visit the sick and accompany medical staff.
Most churches have advised congregants not to shake hands, ban sharing communion cups and placing wafers on the tongue, and stop intinction.

In the UK, the Church of England has advised against intinction and placing wafers on the tongue, suspended physical contact during blessings, and is considering further guidance on Holy Week and Easter services.
The Greek Orthodox church has refused to suspend the ritual of worshippers sipping from the same spoon during Holy Communion, saying it cannot be the cause of the spread of illness.

During Ramadan, mosque attendances usually peak, but Friday prayers have already been suspended across the Middle East, and Saudi Arabia has banned overseas visitors, affecting pilgrims wishing to perform umrah and hajj.
The Muslim Council of Britain has not advised restrictions but warned that could change, expecting mosque committees to follow public health advice, possibly suspending congregational prayers.
Israel has ordered all arrivals from abroad to self-quarantine for 14 days, affecting Jews visiting for Passover and Christian pilgrims visiting holy sites at Easter.

The Conference of European Rabbis has advised against kissing the Torah scroll, and Israel's chief rabbi said people should not touch or kiss mezuzahs; some US synagogues are cancelling events and preparing to livestream services.
Many Hindus in India wore face masks during Holi celebrations, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced he would not take part in public celebrations and advised avoiding large gatherings.
Celebrations for Rama Navami, a public holiday in India, attract thousands of devotees at places associated with Lord Rama.
Gurdwaras are considering postponing events, including nagar kirtans, to mark Vaisakhi, and the Vaisakhi nagar kirtan in Southall has been delayed.

7-36885-6-1.subevent: Mohammed Mostajo-Radji was appointed as Bolivia's first ambassador for science, technology and innovation in February.
He flew back to Bolivia on March 19 at the request of interim president Jeanine Áñez to help coordinate the country's efforts to combat COVID-19.
Mostajo-Radji noted that Bolivia's high altitude is a major challenge because most ventilators don't work appropriately at that level.
He said that large populations live at altitudes above 13,000 feet and only about 30 percent of ventilators actually work there.
While at RIT, Mostajo-Radji developed an interest in science diplomacy and conducted experiments using Real-time polymerase chain reaction for his senior thesis.
He now uses his experience with the equipment to test samples while setting up testing labs in Bolivia.
After earning his degree at RIT, he earned a Ph.D. in cellular and molecular biology at Harvard University in 2017.
He is currently a postdoctoral scholar in regeneration medicine at University of California, San Francisco.
Mostajo-Radji expressed shock at how quickly everything has escalated, saying he would have laughed if asked six months ago if he would be doing this.

9-wiki-img/20320-3/20320-3-1.subevent: Legal scholar Julie Andersen Hill offers solutions to regulatory obstacles preventing marijuana businesses from using financial institutions.
Marijuana business owners must conduct their day-to-day operations entirely in cash because they have little access to banking.
Four states and the District of Columbia allow recreational marijuana use and regulate it in a manner akin to alcohol.
Marijuana is still illegal under federal law, which poses challenges including limiting access to banking.
Individuals and institutions that assist marijuana businesses can be criminally punished as accessories and money launderers.
The U.S. Attorney General issued guidance in 2013 explaining that federal authorities will not prioritize punishing financial institutions working with state-level marijuana industries.
All states require that banks obtain insurance from the FDIC and most require credit unions to acquire insurance from the NCUA, which brings additional federal regulation.
The Federal Reserve can block a bank or credit union's access to payment services if it is associated with marijuana businesses.
The Colorado-chartered Fourth Corner Credit Union filed suit against the Federal Reserve because it was denied a master account.
Colorado passed a bill permitting financial institutions to deal with recreational marijuana businesses, but it requires Federal Reserve approval for payment services.
Hill argues that congressional action is the only feasible solution to the marijuana industry's banking problems.
Representative Ed Perlmutter introduced the Marijuana Business Access to Banking Act of 2015, and Senator Jeff Merkley introduced a companion bill.
Hill contends that federal financial regulators should set clearer and more achievable due diligence standards for banks doing business with marijuana-related companies.

4-35243-6-1.subevent: Amnesty International released a report stating that Eritrean troops killed hundreds of civilians in Axum, Ethiopia, in November last year, amounting to 'a series of human rights and humanitarian law violations'.
The report said that on November 28 and 29, Eritrean troops killed hundreds of civilians in a 'coordinated and systematic' manner to terrorize the population into submission.
Amnesty interviewed 41 witnesses and survivors, all ethnic Tigrayans, who said Eritrean forces carried out extrajudicial executions and engaged in widespread looting.
The violations began on November 19 when Eritrean and Ethiopian forces entered Axum, indiscriminately shelling the city and firing at those who tried to flee.
After the massacre, Eritrean forces detained hundreds of residents and threatened renewed killing if they encountered resistance.
Amnesty said the killings, indiscriminate shelling, and looting 'may amount to war crimes'.
Axum residents identified the perpetrators as Eritrean soldiers, noting they often rode in trucks with licence plates reading 'Eritrea'.
Witnesses said some Eritrean soldiers wore Ethiopian army uniforms but were identified by their plastic shoes known as 'Congo chama' or 'shida'.
Some soldiers had three scars on each temple, marking them as Beni-Amir, an ethnic group straddling Sudan and Eritrea.
The Tigrinya dialect spoken by Eritrean soldiers also distinguished them from Ethiopians.
Ethiopian and Eritrean authorities made contradictory statements about Eritrean troops' involvement in the Tigray conflict.
The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission said Amnesty's report should be taken seriously and that preliminary investigations indicated Eritrean soldiers killed an unknown number of civilians in Axum.
Ethiopia's government denied the presence of Eritrean soldiers in the conflict.
Ethiopia's ambassador to Qatar, Samia Zekaria Gutu, called the Amnesty report 'cooked' and said it risked reinforcing misinformation by the TPLF.
Last month, the US said all soldiers from Eritrea should leave the Tigray region 'immediately'.
Witnesses estimated that Eritrean soldiers number in the thousands, and Eritrean officials did not respond to questions.
Eritrea's information minister tweeted that 'the rabid defamation campaign against Eritrea is on the rise again'.
Amnesty quoted residents saying troops carried out systematic house-to-house raids to kill teenage and adult men.
A man who found refuge in an unfinished building said he saw six Eritrean soldiers kill a neighbour with a vehicle-mounted heavy machine gun near the Mana Hotel.
Another man who returned at night after the shooting stopped said 'all we could see on the streets were dead bodies and people crying'.
In December, UN human rights chief Michelle Bachelet called the situation in Tigray 'exceedingly worrying and volatile' after fighting was reported in areas surrounding Mekelle, Sheraro, and Axum.
Bachelet said the UN had corroborated information of gross human rights violations including indiscriminate attacks, looting, abductions, and sexual violence.
The conflict left thousands dead and caused some 950,000 to flee their homes.
Little is known about the situation for most of Tigray's six million people because many journalists and aid workers have been blocked from entering and communications are patchy.

6-19228-1-1.subevent: Some of America's most deeply held secrets may have been stolen in a monthslong operation blamed on elite Russian government hackers.

U.S. government agencies, including the Treasury and Commerce departments, were among dozens of high-value targets infiltrated as far back as March through a commercial software update from SolarWinds.
A Pentagon statement indicated it used the software and had issued guidance and directives to protect its networks, but would not say whether any systems may have been hacked.
Acting Defense Secretary Chris Miller told CBS News there was so far no evidence of compromise.
The hackers carefully exfiltrated data, often encrypting it, and expertly covered their tracks.

Thomas Rid, a Johns Hopkins cyberconflict expert, compared the campaign's likely efficacy to Russia's 1990s 'Moonlight Maze' hacking and estimated the stolen documents could be several Washington Monument piles.
The Trump administration has not said which agencies were hacked, and no private-sector victims have come forward.
President Donald Trump's national security adviser, Robert O'Brien, cut short an overseas trip to hold meetings on the hack and was to convene a top-level interagency meeting later this week.
The White House said a coordinating team had been created to respond, including the FBI, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
At a briefing for congressional staffers, DHS did not say how many agencies were hacked, reflecting how little the Trump administration has been sharing with Congress.

Critics complained that the Trump administration failed to address cybersecurity threats, and Trump eliminated two key government positions: White House cybersecurity coordinator and State Department cybersecurity policy chief.
Hackers infiltrated government agencies by piggybacking malicious code on SolarWinds software beginning in March.
The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity company FireEye when it detected it had been hacked, and it disclosed the breach Dec. 8 and alerted the FBI and other federal agencies.
FireEye executive Charles Carmakal said it was aware of 'dozens of incredibly high-value targets' infiltrated and expected many more to learn they were compromised.
The SolarWinds campaign highlighted the lack of mandatory minimum security rules for commercial software used on federal computer networks.
Rep. Jim Langevin said the breach reminded him of the 2015 Chinese hack of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management and highlighted the need for a national cyber director at the White House.
Trump threatened to veto the defense bill over objections to unrelated provisions.

1-16514-5-1.subevent: A hacking group linked to the Iranian government attempted to break into U.S. President Donald Trump's re-election campaign but was unsuccessful.

Microsoft Corp said it saw significant cyber activity by the group, which also targeted current and former U.S. government officials, journalists covering global politics, and prominent Iranians living outside Iran.
The Trump campaign's Director of Communications Tim Murtaugh said there was no indication that any of the campaign's infrastructure was targeted.
In a 30-day period between August and September, the group made more than 2,700 attempts to identify consumer email accounts and attacked 241 of those accounts.
Microsoft said four accounts were compromised, but they were not associated with the U.S. presidential campaign or current and former U.S. government officials.
Microsoft's blog post did not identify the election campaign whose network was targeted.
Tensions between the United States and Iran have risen since May 2018 when Trump withdrew from a 2015 international nuclear accord with Tehran.
The Iranian government did not issue any immediate comment through state-run media on Microsoft's statement.
Microsoft said Phosphorous used information gathered from researching targets to game password reset or account recovery features and attempt to take over some targeted accounts.
Microsoft has been tracking Phosphorus since 2013 and said in March that it had received a court order to take control of 99 websites the group used to execute attacks.
A computer network used by 2016 Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton's campaign was hacked in a cyberattack on Democratic Party political organizations in that U.S. election.
Companies including Facebook Inc, Alphabet Inc's Google, Microsoft and Twitter Inc met with U.S. intelligence agencies earlier in September to discuss security strategies.

Microsoft had said in a blog post in July that about 10,000 customers were targeted or compromised by nation-state attacks in the past year, with most activity originating from Iran, North Korea, and Russia.

35-5391-7-1.subevent: NATO took the lead of the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) in Afghanistan on 11 August 2003.

ISAF's primary objective was to enable the Afghan government to provide effective security across the country and develop new Afghan security forces to ensure Afghanistan would never again become a safe haven for terrorists.
From 2011, responsibility for security was gradually transitioned to Afghan forces, which took the lead for security operations across the country by summer 2013.
The transition process was completed and Afghan forces assumed full security responsibility at the end of 2014, when the ISAF mission was completed.
A new, smaller non-combat mission ('Resolute Support') was launched on 1 January 2015 to provide further training, advice and assistance to the Afghan security forces and institutions.
ISAF was one of the largest coalitions in history and is NATO's most challenging mission to date, with more than 130,000 troops from 51 NATO and partner nations at its height.
Originally deployed to provide security in and around Kabul, ISAF's presence was gradually expanded to cover the whole country by the second half of 2006.
As ISAF expanded into the east and south, its troops became increasingly engaged in fighting a growing insurgency in 2007 and 2008, while trying to help Afghanistan rebuild.
In 2009, a new counter-insurgency was launched and 40,000 extra troops were deployed.
ISAF assisted the Afghan National Security Forces (ANSF) in the conduct of security operations throughout the country, helping to reduce the capability of the insurgency.

An important priority for ISAF was to increase the capacity and capabilities of the Afghan forces, which became the main focus of the mission from 2011 onwards as ISAF shifted from a combat-centric role to training, advising and assisting.
The multinational force also helped to create the space and lay the foundations for improvements in governance and socio-economic development for sustainable stability.

2-34830-6-t.subevent: A boat carrying three dozen Syrian refugees approaches the Greek island of Lesbos, with shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' heard.
More than 124,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year.
The United Nations urged Greece to take control of the 'total chaos' hitting the islands, with a UNHCR official calling the situation 'shameful'.
Greek Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras asked Europe for help handling the influx, saying the boatloads of migrants were triggering a 'humanitarian crisis within the economic crisis'.
At least six dinghies make the same approach to the shoreline in just hours.
The refugees cheer and snap selfies as they approach the shore.
The refugees clambered out as the boat hit the shore, and one woman collapsed in tears on her knees in the sand.
The refugees must walk miles to the island's capital to register with authorities.
A day earlier, police processed more than 1,200 arrivals.

17-27606-1-3.subevent: Chris Mosier grew up in Midwest America feeling confident as an athlete, with his athletic ability being the only distinction between him and other athletes.
In 2016, Mosier qualified for the Team USA roster at the sprint duathlon national championship, becoming the first out transgender man to make a U.S. National Team.

After coming out as a trans athlete, Mosier faced barriers such as inaccessible locker rooms, being denied admission to a pool, and being unable to use a restroom at a Team USA qualifying race in North Carolina due to HB2 law.
Mosier became a competitive triathlete and duathlete after college, having previously stayed busy during college to avoid conversations about his identity.
Mosier met his wife Zhen Heinemann, and through their relationship he began to figure out his sexuality and gender identity, eventually identifying as queer.
In 2010, Mosier began his transition, taking testosterone, changing his gender designation on documents, and competing in men's triathlons and duathlons.
Mosier was inspired by Tommie Smith and aimed to be a role model for young trans athletes.
Due to regulatory changes from the IOC and other governing bodies, trans athletes who have undergone hormone therapy for one year and pass TUE tests are allowed to compete without restriction.
Before the new IOC policy was enacted in January 2016, Mosier and other trans athletes were ineligible for international and national competition for nearly six months.

The IOC regulations require transgender women to have testosterone levels below 10 nmol/L for at least 12 months before competing, and transgender men must undergo lab tests and annual reports to compete under TUE.
No trans athlete has dominated a sport on the national or international level, and public commentary on transgender athletes like Naataphon Wangyot has been negative.

Mosier believes that the two trans athletes at Rio are not coming out publicly due to the lack of normalization of trans athletes, and he hopes that one day being a transgender man will be seen as a benign fact.
Mosier continues to train, speak out publicly, advocate for LGBT athletes, and comply with testing regulations, aiming to make the playing field equal for others.

0-4495-1-4.subevent: Tunisia Youth Impact uses cooking contests to encourage young Tunisian women in rural villages to vote in the presidential election.
On October 12, a cooking contest is held in Echamine, a rural town south of Tunis, the day before the second round of the presidential election.
The national turnout in the first round was 48.98%.
Tunisia Youth Impact's Voticook contests aim to raise awareness among rural populations, especially women, about participating in democracy.
The contest simulates real voting conditions, with volunteers matching electoral procedures and using water and shampoo instead of ink.
Hinda Jlass, a mother of four, prepares couscous for the competition and says the event is a way to get together with other women.
Hinda Jlass plans to vote in the presidential election the next day, which would be only the second time she has voted in her life.
Seven women compete in the contest, presenting dishes to about fifty electors.
The electors taste the dishes and vote using the same procedure as in the presidential election, with volunteers guiding them.
Members of the Tunisian election authority and EU observer Stefan Ziegler attend the event, with Ziegler saying it is original and good for democracy.
After the vote, volunteers point out mistakes that could invalidate a vote, such as signing instead of crossing.
Najwa Jlass, the sister of the hostess, wins the contest and says she will vote 'for real' the next day.

1-15363-1-2.subevent: Petra Kvitova defeated Laura Siegemund 6-3 6-3 to reach her second French Open semi-final.
Kvitova reached the semi-finals at Roland Garros for the first time since 2012.
Kvitova made an emotional return to professional tennis at Roland Garros three years after a burglar attack damaged her left hand.
Kvitova said she didn't dream of being in a semi-final after everything that happened and called Roland Garros her lucky place.
Siegemund was appearing in the second week of a Grand Slam for the first time in her career.
Kvitova dominated the first set, hitting six aces and converting her first breakpoint opportunity to win it in 34 minutes.
In the second set, Siegemund fought back, saving breakpoints and breaking Kvitova to level at 2-2.
Siegemund lost her cool at the umpire after a time violation warning and suffered another break.
Siegemund called the trainer for a lower back massage and broke back to level the set.
Kvitova got the decisive break and converted her second match point when Siegemund double-faulted.
Kvitova will face the winner of the match between Danielle Collins and Sofia Kenin in the semi-finals.

4-35559-2-1.subevent: Rabobank economists released their quarterly report stating that the Dutch economy is facing its deepest dip in a hundred years despite coronavirus support packages.
Rabobank expects the Dutch economy to shrink by nearly 6 percent this year, but notes the Netherlands is better off than many other European countries.
Rabobank expects the economy shrunk by 8 percent between March and early June, with the catering industry hit particularly hard.

Rabobank's Ester Barendregt said that restaurants and cafes are allowed to open again, causing the catering industry to pick up somewhat, but a contraction of 41 percent remains for the sector for the year as a whole.
Barendregt said the biggest blow to industry is likely to come in the third quarter, and construction will be delayed by the corona crisis and nitrogen problems, with shrinkage continuing into 2021.

Rabobank expects unemployment to rise from 3 percent at the start of the year to 7 percent by the end of this year, with more self-employed, freelancers, and permanent employees losing jobs due to reorganizations and bankruptcies.
Rabobank said Dutch companies will export 7.2 percent less goods and services this year due to the pandemic and weakened demand from trading partners.

Barendregt said the corona crisis is a huge blow to the Dutch economy, but Dutch expectations are relatively mild compared to other eurozone countries due to the intelligent lockdown, good economic shape, and high digitization.
Rabobank expects the Dutch economy to grow again next year by 2.9 percent.

Rabobank expects France, Italy, and the United Kingdom to see their economies shrink by over 10 percent this year, but grow by 7 to 8 percent next year, partly due to their less deep fall and the Netherlands' vulnerability to a drop in demand from abroad.

6-19273-8-t.subevent: A man named Robin Lee was told he would be arrested if he refused to unplug his iPhone from a socket on the London Overground, and he was arrested, only to be de-arrested later.
19-year-old Nick Silvestri jumped on a Broadway stage and tried to jam his phone in a prop outlet because it was on 5% and girls were calling all day.
A 2012 study shows that 77% of young Americans are nomophobes, a condition suffered by 66% of the British population.
An unnamed woman was filmed on public transport in Hong Kong dealing with her dead phone by screaming and crying for help.

13-24655-1-1.subevent: Pope Francis prayed for peace and dialogue in Paraguay during his General Audience.
The Pope expressed concern over the situation in Paraguay and invoked the intercession of Our Lady of Miracles of Caacupé.
The Pope asked the Lord Jesus, Prince of Peace, for a path of sincere dialogue to find adequate solutions to the current difficulties.

Church leaders in Paraguay appealed for calm and called for a national dialogue in the face of the crisis worsened by rising Covid infections and economic stress.

Bradbrook attempted to smash a ministry window with a hammer and screwdriver before being arrested by police.
Extinction Rebellion staged protest actions in cities worldwide since October 7, including in New York and Brussels.
Police ordered a halt to all Extinction Rebellion protests in London on Monday, threatening arrests for non-compliance.
Around 1,500 arrests were made in London over eight days, with more than 1,400 arrests in other countries.
The British government supported the police call, saying protests should not disrupt daily life.
An activist attempted to lock herself to the ministry, criticizing HS2 for destroying habitats.
Police began arresting activists blocking a road near MI5 headquarters to highlight climate risks to food security.
London police's Deputy Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said robust action would be taken against unlawful protests.
Extinction Rebellion claimed HS2 would damage or destroy 108 ancient woodlands, while the transport ministry said 7 million new trees would be planted.

Kvitova reached her second semi-final at the French Open, eight years after her first in 2012.

Kvitova reflected on her emotional return to tennis after a burglary attack in 2016 that injured her left hand.
Siegemund was appearing in the second week of a Grand Slam for the first time in her career.
Kvitova dominated the first set, hitting six aces and converting her first breakpoint to win it in 34 minutes.

3-18013-3-t.subevent: China recovered precious lunar samples after a successful reentry and landing of the Chang’e-5 return capsule.

Chang’e-5 launched Nov. 23, entering lunar orbit 112 hours later, and sampling followed after a Dec. 1 landing, with an ascent vehicle delivering collected material into lunar orbit.
An unprecedented automated lunar orbit rendezvous and docking with the mission service module two days later allowed the transfer of 2 kilograms of material into the return capsule.

Sample return technology and experience from Chang’e-5 will be utilized for planned near Earth asteroid and Mars sample return missions later in the decade.

1-15313-3-t.subevent: A group of 20 top virus experts from the US, UK, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere said the coronavirus pandemic almost certainly originated from an animal, probably at a wildlife market in China, and not from a laboratory leak.
